# How to make Laravel (Blade) text field readonly

When building forms in Laravel, there are scenarios where you need to display a value that the user cannot edit, yet the application still needs to process that specific input. A common use case is generating a one-time login token or a reset password code and displaying it in an input field so the user can copy it, but preventing them from accidentally modifying it before submission.

The standard HTML attribute for this behavior is `readonly`. While `disabled` prevents interaction entirely and excludes the field from the form data submitted via a POST request, `readonly` allows the browser to capture the value and include it in the form submission while strictly forbidding user edits. In Laravel's Blade syntax, you cannot simply drop the `readonly` attribute onto a standard helper call like `{!! Form::text(...) !!}` without careful attention to how the attributes are passed through.

### Using Helper Attributes

Laravel's form helpers support passing an array of HTML attributes directly into the field generation method. To apply the `readonly` property, you pass it as part of the attributes array alongside your value.

If you are using the older `Form::open` syntax, which returns a `FormBuilder` instance that allows for chaining, you can append the attribute like this:

```php
{{ Form::text('login_token', Worker::generateLoginToken(), ['readonly' => true]) }}
```

Here, the first argument is the field name, the second is the default value (or an empty string if omitted), and the third is an associative array of attributes. By setting `'readonly' => true`, Laravel's underlying HTML generator will correctly output `readonly="readonly"` in the resulting HTML. This ensures that when the form is submitted, the value generated by `Worker::generateLoginToken()` is included in your controller's `$request` object as expected.

### Handling Security and Validation

It is important to distinguish between `readonly` and `disabled`. If you use the `'disabled' => true` attribute, the browser will not send the field's value with the form submission at all. This breaks the requirement of having PHP process that specific input. With `readonly`, the user cannot type into the box, but the backend logic remains fully aware of the content because the data is still present in the HTTP POST payload.

This distinction becomes critical during validation. When you run `$request->validate(['login_token' => 'required', ...])`, Laravel expects the `login_token` key to exist in the input array. If you accidentally used a disabled field, that key would be missing, causing a validation failure unless you explicitly handle its absence. Using the `readonly` attribute preserves this key-value pair, maintaining the integrity of your request validation rules.

### Avoiding Common Pitfalls

A frequent mistake when manually inserting HTML attributes in Blade is forgetting to escape the output or relying on double curly braces `{{ }}`. While the form helpers generally handle escaping correctly when passed a value, if you were to switch to raw HTML generation using `{!! !!}`, you must ensure your generated value is safe. Since `Worker::generateLoginToken()` produces a server-side string, it should not contain user input that requires further sanitization before being placed inside an attribute or value context, but always verify the source of your data.

Another consideration involves CSS styling. Some themes might style `input[type="text"]` to look different when disabled versus readonly. Since you are explicitly opting for `readonly`, ensure your stylesheet does not inadvertently inherit styles meant for disabled fields, such as greyed-out text, which could confuse users about the field's purpose.

For more complex scenarios involving dynamic attributes or custom HTML generation within Laravel forms, checking out resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can provide additional context on advanced form handling strategies and best practices for specific Laravel versions.
